description: The Adaptive Systems Research Institute studies AI systems that adapt to the people and settings they work with, and methods for testing that those systems do what they are meant to do. An adaptive system changes what it does based on feedback from the setting it works in. The institute's research areas cover how adaptive systems are built, the fields where the institute applies them, and how they are evaluated.

details:
Rice Pulse uses a year of radar from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite to show when rice fields along the Colorado River of Texas are flooded, and how much land is under water, every twelve days.

The Lower Colorado River Authority releases water from Lake Buchanan and Lake Travis to irrigate rice in Colorado, Wharton and Matagorda counties. Those lakes also supply Austin. In dry years the two uses compete: during the 2012–2015 drought, most of that irrigation water was cut off to protect the lakes. Growers, water managers and the city all need to know when fields are flooded. Optical satellites need clear skies to see them, but NISAR’s L-band radar sees through cloud and works at night.

Two consecutive frames of one NISAR orbit (track 62, frames 16 and 17) cover the corridor from the Highland Lakes to Matagorda Bay. We used all 29 passes from November 2, 2025 to October 28, 2026. For each pass we join the two frames into one map, filter out radar speckle, and map two surfaces in a 9,178 km² area over the rice belt:

  • Open water, which reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite and appears dark.
  • Rice standing in flooded paddies. The pulse bounces off the water, then off the stems, straight back to the satellite, so these fields show bright magenta.

The results run in an interactive 3D globe in the browser, built on the open-source God’s Eye View. A slider plays through the passes. Four views show the radar image, the mapped water, the change since the first pass and how often each field was under water. A chart follows both surfaces through the year.

The rice season is easy to see. Rice standing in water grew from about 470 km² in late May to 1,367 km² on July 12. It fell to 148 km² on August 17, when the main crop was drained for harvest. Through September and October it came back to 370–650 km² as the second (ratoon) crop grew. The largest open-water reading, 1,935 km² on March 26, was rain standing on saturated ground, not fields flooded for rice.

This version uses NISAR’s public preview images, at about 173 m per pixel. At that size it can’t yet measure narrow reservoirs like Lake Travis. NISAR’s full calibrated data has about 20 m pixels. With that data and field boundaries, the same pipeline could estimate flooded acreage every week for each irrigation district. It could warn early when demand on the lakes rises in a dry year, and give water-allocation and crop-insurance decisions evidence that doesn’t depend on clear skies.

Built with Python for the data processing, the NASA ASF DAAC search API for the NISAR data, and JavaScript with CesiumJS on God’s Eye View for the app, over Esri World Imagery. Live at https://rice-pulse.adaptivesystems.institute.
